body:
Birsa Munda and the Chotanagpur region

Birsa Munda was born on 15 November 1875 at Ulihatu in the Chotanagpur region, now in Jharkhand. He belonged to the Munda community and became an influential religious and political leader. His followers honoured him with titles including Dharti Aba, meaning Father of the Earth.

During Birsa's lifetime, many Mundas faced difficulties arising from altered land arrangements and the growing influence of landlords and moneylenders. Traditional claims to ancestral land, including those associated with the khuntkatti system of customary Munda landholding, were under pressure.

Birsa's programme of social and religious reform

Birsa's teachings were shaped by his experiences of tribal traditions, missionary education and Vaishnav religious preaching. He urged followers to improve community life through moral discipline.

His social reform programme included:

  • Abandoning the consumption of liquor.
  • Keeping villages clean.
  • Rejecting witchcraft, sorcery and practices he regarded as harmful.
  • Restoring dignity and unity within the community.

The religious movement associated with his teachings came to be known as the Birsait movement. It was not simply an adoption of Christianity or Vaishnavism. Birsa drew on ideas he had encountered while developing a distinctive programme directed at the needs of his followers.

The vision of a golden age

Birsa spoke of a past satyug, or golden age, when the Mundas lived without the oppression of outsiders, worked their own land and followed an honest, orderly way of life. This vision gave religious meaning to the demand for the restoration of ancestral rights.

His political objective was often expressed as the establishment of Munda Raj: a form of self-rule free from the domination of the colonial government and exploitative outsiders. Thus, Birsa's message combined religious purification, community reform, agrarian rights and political resistance.

From reform to the Ulgulan

Birsa's activities drew the attention of British authorities. He was arrested in 1895 and imprisoned. After his release in 1897, he resumed organising followers.

The movement developed into the Ulgulan, meaning the Great Tumult or Great Rebellion, during 1899–1900. Followers challenged symbols of colonial and outsider authority. Birsa was arrested again and died in British custody on 9 June 1900.

Although the movement was suppressed, it drew attention to the problem of land alienation. The later Chotanagpur Tenancy Act, 1908, placed restrictions on transfers of land and became an important measure associated with the protection of customary and tribal land rights in the region. The Act was enacted after Birsa's death; it was not a law introduced by him.

Prelims focus

  • Birsa Munda: Munda leader of Chotanagpur, born at Ulihatu on 15 November 1875.
  • Dharti Aba: an honorific associated with Birsa Munda.
  • 1895: Birsa was arrested; 1897: he resumed organising after release.
  • Ulgulan: the Birsa-led movement of 1899–1900.
  • 1908: Chotanagpur Tenancy Act, a later measure concerning land rights.
  • Trap: Birsa's movement was both socio-religious and political; it was not confined to religious worship.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 8, Our Pasts–III, chapter 'Tribals, Dikus and the Vision of a Golden Age', printed pp. 39 and 48–49; Press Information Bureau, About 'Bhagwan' Birsa Munda, November 2021, sections on his life, social reform and the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act; Press Information Bureau, New India Samachar, November 2022, feature 'Bhagwan Birsa Munda: Dharti Aaba'.]

pictures.alt: Munda villagers of different ages discuss community concerns near mud homes and cultivated fields in forested Chotanagpur.
pictures.caption: Village gatherings helped connect religious teaching with the protection of ancestral land in Chotanagpur.

pictures.alt: Religious reform and ancestral land rights converge in Munda Raj and the Ulgulan, followed by Birsa's death and later land-protection legislation.
pictures.caption: Birsa's movement combined religious reform, land-rights demands and political resistance.

title: Birsa Munda: Religious Renewal, Munda Raj and the Ulgulan

body:
Origin among the Oraons

The Tana Bhagat movement began in 1914 among the Oraon community of the Chotanagpur region. Its early leader was Jatra Oraon, also known as Jatra Bhagat, who came from the Gumla area of present-day Jharkhand.

Jatra claimed to have received a religious message from Dharmes, the supreme divine figure in the Oraon religious tradition. He called upon followers to change their social and religious practices and free themselves from oppressive relationships.

The programme of religious and social purification

The movement encouraged followers to reject spirit-related practices, witchcraft accusations, animal sacrifice and alcohol consumption. It emphasised moral discipline, simplicity, purity and a more orderly religious life.

The Tana Bhagats also challenged established relations of dependence. Their early demands included resistance to unpaid labour and opposition to the authority of exploitative landlords and moneylenders. Thus, the movement was rooted in both religious reform and agrarian grievances.

Birsa Munda belonged to the Munda community; Jatra Oraon belonged to the Oraon community. Both movements arose in the Chotanagpur region, but they had different leaders, dates and organisational histories.

Relationship with Gandhian nationalism

The Tana Bhagat movement began before the major Gandhian mass movements in India. It was therefore not founded by Mahatma Gandhi.

In the early 1920s, sections of the Tana Bhagat community developed close links with the nationalist movement. Practices associated with peaceful protest, refusal to cooperate with exploitative authority and disciplined collective action helped create points of connection with Gandhian politics. Tana Bhagats participated in Non-Cooperation activities and adopted symbols such as khadi and the national movement's flag.

This later association does not change the movement's original character. Its first phase was an Oraon religious and social reform movement that also expressed dissatisfaction with existing agrarian relations.

Prelims focus

  • 1914: beginning of the Tana Bhagat movement.
  • Founder: Jatra Oraon, also called Jatra Bhagat.
  • Community: Oraon; region: Chotanagpur.
  • The movement opposed liquor, animal sacrifice and exploitative labour relationships.
  • Sections of the movement later joined Gandhian Non-Cooperation activities.
  • Trap: The Tana Bhagat movement originated in 1914; Gandhi did not establish it.

[Sources: Sangeeta Dasgupta, 'Reordering a World: The Tana Bhagat Movement, 1914–1919', Studies in History, vol. 15, no. 1, 1999, pp. 1–8 and discussion of the movement's early practices; Census of India, District Census Handbook: Ranchi, 2011, district history, printed p. 14; Sangeeta Dasgupta, 'Reading Adivasi Histories: Tana Bhagats in Colonial Times', sections on the movement's first phase and its links with nationalism.]

pictures.alt: Jatra Oraon founded the Tana Bhagat movement in 1914; sections joined Gandhian nationalism in the early 1920s. Gandhi was not its founder.
pictures.caption: The Tana Bhagat movement began as Oraon community reform and later became connected with the national movement.

title: Jatra Oraon and the Tana Bhagat Movement

body:
Govind Guru and the Bhil communities

Govind Guru, also called Govindgiri, was a religious and social reformer associated with the Bhil communities of southern Rajasthan and the neighbouring regions of Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh.

His activities were especially important in the former princely-state areas of Banswara, Dungarpur and Sunth and adjoining Bhil-inhabited territories. This makes the movement relevant to the history of both Rajasthan and Gujarat.

The Bhagat movement and Samp Sabha

Govind Guru encouraged a programme of moral and social discipline. His followers were urged to abstain from intoxicants, reject harmful practices, maintain community solidarity and improve their conduct. Religious observances associated with the movement included tending a dhuni, or sacred fire.

He was closely associated with the Samp Sabha, an organisation that helped bring followers together and spread reformist teachings. The broader movement is often described as the Bhil Bhagat movement.

These efforts addressed social behaviour, but they also helped Bhils organise against the burdens imposed by landlords, officials and princely authorities. Demands concerning unpaid labour, taxes and oppressive treatment gave the movement a political and economic dimension.

The Mangarh gathering of 1913

Mangarh Hill is in the Banswara region of present-day Rajasthan, close to the Gujarat border. It became an important gathering place for Govind Guru's Bhil followers.

On 17 November 1913, forces associated with British authority and the princely states attacked the Bhil gathering at Mangarh. The event is remembered as the Mangarh massacre. Historical accounts differ substantially in their estimates of the number of people killed; the date, location, association with Govind Guru and the attack on the gathering are the central facts to retain.

The incident illustrates how a movement beginning with religious purification and social discipline could develop into confrontation with established political authority.

Prelims focus

  • Govind Guru or Govindgiri: associated with the Bhil Bhagat movement.
  • Samp Sabha: organisation associated with Govind Guru's movement.
  • Dhuni: sacred fire associated with followers' religious practices.
  • 17 November 1913: Mangarh massacre.
  • Mangarh: present-day Rajasthan, near the Gujarat border.
  • Trap: Mangarh was a major centre for a movement relevant to Gujarat, but the hill lies in present-day Rajasthan.

[Sources: Ministry of Culture, Government of India, Dictionary of Martyrs: India's Freedom Struggle, 1857–1947, vol. 2, part 1, printed p. 189, entry concerning the Bhagat Bhil movement; Press Information Bureau, 'Mangarh Dham ki Gaurav Gatha', 1 November 2022, background on Govind Guru and the Mangarh gathering; 'Subalterns and the State in the Longue Durée: Notes from The Rebellious Century in the Bhil Heartland', Journal of Contemporary Asia, section 'Bhil Resistance in the Rajputana Agency'.]

pictures.alt: Govind Guru’s reforms united Bhils through Samp Sabha; grievances over exploitation drove organised opposition before the Mangarh attack on 17 November 1913.
pictures.caption: The Bhil movement under Govind Guru developed from moral reform into organised opposition to exploitation.

title: Govind Guru, the Bhil Bhagat Movement and Mangarh

body:
Origin and regional setting

The Devi movement was an important socio-religious movement among Adivasi communities of South Gujarat in 1922–1923. It spread through parts of the former Surat region and adjoining tribal areas, including areas associated with Vyara, Bardoli, Valod, Valsad and the Dangs.

The movement became particularly significant among the Chodhris, also written as Chaudharis, and other Adivasi groups of South Gujarat. It did not have one central founder comparable to Birsa Munda or Govind Guru.

The teachings associated with Salabai

Participants believed that a divine power known as Salabai, also written as Salahbai, communicated instructions through religious mediums. Gatherings brought people together to hear these messages and commit themselves to changed social conduct.

The principal instructions included:

  • Giving up liquor and toddy.
  • Abstaining from meat and avoiding animal sacrifice.
  • Bathing regularly and maintaining personal cleanliness.
  • Keeping houses and villages clean.
  • Observing collective discipline and following the movement's moral rules.

These demands gave the movement the character of a religious purification campaign. At the same time, its collective practices strengthened solidarity among participating Adivasi communities.

Why abstinence also became economic resistance

In parts of South Gujarat, some Parsi liquor and toddy dealers were also involved in moneylending, landholding or other relationships of economic dependence. The movement's demand to give up liquor therefore affected more than personal consumption. It also encouraged participants to avoid particular traders and challenge exploitative relationships.

In some areas, the movement included a social boycott of Parsi liquor dealers and landlords. This should be understood in its historical and economic setting. It was not the same as the Parsi religious reform movement in Bombay, nor does it justify treating every Parsi individual as an exploiter.

Two different historical contexts

Parsi reform of 1851 involved members of the Parsi community seeking religious and social change within their community. The Devi movement of 1922–1923 involved Adivasi communities in South Gujarat, some of whose participants opposed the economic power of particular Parsi liquor dealers. The shared reference to Parsis does not make these the same movement.

Connection with Gandhian activity

The Devi movement developed during a period when Gandhian ideas of abstinence, self-discipline and non-cooperation were also circulating in Gujarat. Some of its participants subsequently became associated with nationalist activity, khadi and constructive work.

However, the movement's religious origin and local Adivasi leadership should be distinguished from its later links with Gandhian politics. Mahatma Gandhi was not its founder.

Prelims focus

  • 1922–1923: the Devi movement in South Gujarat.
  • Salabai: the divine figure whose instructions participants believed were transmitted through mediums.
  • Chodhris: among the important participating Adivasi communities.
  • Core practices included abstinence from liquor and toddy, cleanliness and collective discipline.
  • The movement also challenged particular Parsi liquor dealers and other exploitative economic relationships.
  • Trap: The Devi movement was not founded by Gandhi and was not a Parsi religious reform organisation.

[Sources: David Hardiman, The Coming of the Devi: Adivasi Assertion in Western India, Oxford University Press, 1987, chapters 'Origins and Transformations of the Devi', 'The Message' and 'The Devi and Gandhi'; IGNOU, Anti-Colonial Tribal Movements in India, Unit 15, section 15.5.6, 'Devi Movement in Gujarat (1922–23)', printed pp. 55–56; Rash Bihari Lal, Socio-Religious Movements among Tribals of South Gujarat, Tribal Research and Training Institute, Gujarat Vidyapith, 1977, section 'Devi Movement', printed pp. 10–12.]

pictures.alt: Salabai’s religious instructions led to Adivasi solidarity and economic boycott; some participants later joined Gandhian nationalist activity.
pictures.caption: Religious instructions in the Devi movement could produce social reform and economic resistance at the same time.

title: The Devi Movement of South Gujarat, 1922–1923
